newsitem.title: UK: EU sugar quotas unchanged up to 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: EU sugar quotas unchanged up to 1997/98.

text.p: The European Union (EU) is unlikely to reduce sugar production quotas for its member states in the short term but cuts could be seen by the year 2000 if world prices are very low, a key EU official said on Thursday.

Ejner Stendevad, head of sugar at the EU's Directorate General for Agriculture, said export constraints under the General Agreement on Tariffs and trade (GATT() could lead to quota reductions but not before 1998/99.
Speaking at a two-day conference hosted by Agra Europe, he said the impact was related to the level of consumption.
But while forecasts did not indicate a need for quota cuts before 1998/99 he added that problems could arise in 1999/2000 if world prices were very low.
"When we are not using the quotas to the full, it is to our advantage. For the next marketing year there are no difficulties," he said.

In 1995/96 the EU saw a total 464,487 tonnes of unused quota tonnage, mainly from France's overseas territories known as DOM (Departements Outre Mer). Italy could also have produced over 100,000 tonnes more sugar in 1995/96.

Stendevad said the EU's quotas dating from 1981 were, in principle, left unchanged up to the end of the century but could in practice be reduced for a given marketing year according to GATT requirements.

Temporary difficulties could be solved by increasing sugar stocks, he said. But the EU would have to stimulate consumption and utilise its agricultural potential to the full to avoid quota cuts. "The only element we have, besides production which we cannot reduce, is to stimulate consumption. We should do everything we can," Stendevad said.
